# Configure GPU Support in a Target Environment

This guide explains how to validate NVIDIA GPU support on a K3s target environment and how to enable GPU workloads for Villanova deployments.

## Prerequisites

- A K3s target environment already configured for Villanova.
- An NVIDIA GPU installed on at least one node.
- NVIDIA drivers already installed on the host.
- `kubectl` access to the cluster.
- `helm` installed on the administration host.

## 1. Verify GPU Support on the Host

Check that the node sees the GPU:

```bash
nvidia-smi
```

Expected result: the command prints the GPU model, driver version, and CUDA version without errors.

Verify that the NVIDIA container toolkit is available:

```bash
nvidia-container-toolkit --version
```

Expected result: the command prints the installed toolkit version.

## 2. Verify the NVIDIA Runtime in K3s

Check that the NVIDIA runtime is registered in the active containerd configuration:

```bash
  sudo grep -A3 "nvidia" /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml
```

Expected result:

```toml
[plugins.'io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime'.containerd.runtimes.'nvidia']
[plugins.'io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime'.containerd.runtimes.'nvidia'.options]
  BinaryName = "/usr/bin/nvidia-container-runtime"
```

If the runtime is missing, also inspect the K3s containerd template:

```bash
sudo cat /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml.tmpl
sudo ls -la /etc/containerd/conf.d/
```

On K3s installations that use `imports = ["/etc/containerd/conf.d/*.toml"]`, an empty `/etc/containerd/conf.d/` directory can prevent the NVIDIA runtime from being configured as expected.

## 3. Set the Default Runtime in K3s

Update the K3s configuration file:

```yaml
write-kubeconfig-mode: "0600"
disable:
  - servicelb
tls-san:
  - "<PUBLIC_IP>"
node-name: "<NODE_NAME>"
default-runtime: nvidia
```

File: `/etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml`

Restart K3s after the change.

## 4. Configure CDI Classes and Containerd Runtime

Create the CDI directory and generate both workload and management CDI classes:

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /etc/cdi

# Workload class
sudo nvidia-ctk cdi generate --output=/etc/cdi/nvidia.yaml

# Management class (used internally by the device plugin)
sudo nvidia-ctk cdi generate --vendor=management.nvidia.com --class=gpu --output=/etc/cdi/management.yaml
```

Verify both classes are present:

```bash
sudo nvidia-ctk cdi list
```

Expected result: entries for both `nvidia.com/gpu=*` and `management.nvidia.com/gpu=*` are listed.

Ensure the NVIDIA runtime stanza exists in the K3s containerd template:

```bash
sudo cp /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml \
  /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml.tmpl

sudo tee -a /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml.tmpl > /dev/null <<'EOF'
[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.nvidia]
runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v2"
[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.nvidia.options]
BinaryName = "/usr/bin/nvidia-container-runtime"
EOF
```

Restart K3s:

```bash
sudo systemctl restart k3s
```

## 5. Create the NVIDIA RuntimeClass

Apply the runtime class used by GPU workloads:

```bash
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: nvidia
handler: nvidia
EOF
```

Verify that it exists:

```bash
kubectl get runtimeclass
```

Expected result: a `RuntimeClass` named `nvidia` is listed.

## 6. Install the NVIDIA GPU Operator

Add the NVIDIA Helm repository and update the index:

```bash
helm repo add nvidia https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia
helm repo update
```

Install the operator with K3s-friendly settings:

```bash
helm install --wait --generate-name \
  -n gpu-operator --create-namespace \
  nvidia/gpu-operator \
  --version=v26.3.3 \
  --set driver.enabled=false \
  --set cdi.enabled=true \
  --set cdi.default=true \
  --set toolkit.env[0].name=CONTAINERD_RUNTIME_CLASS \
  --set toolkit.env[0].value=nvidia
```

This configuration assumes the NVIDIA driver is already managed on the host and only the Kubernetes GPU components need to be deployed.

## 7. Install the NVIDIA Device Plugin

If you are not using the full GPU Operator stack, install the NVIDIA device plugin directly:

```bash
helm repo add nvdp https://nvidia.github.io/k8s-device-plugin
helm repo update
helm install nvdp nvdp/nvidia-device-plugin --namespace kube-system --create-namespace
```

## 8. Validate GPU Scheduling

Run a test workload:

```bash
kubectl run gpu-test --rm -it --restart=Never \
  --image=nvidia/cuda:12.4.0-base-ubuntu22.04 \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":"nvidia"}}' \
  -- nvidia-smi
```

Expected result: the pod starts successfully and prints `nvidia-smi` output from inside the container.

You can also validate allocatable GPU resources:

```bash
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq '.items[].status.allocatable'
```

Expected result: at least one node exposes `nvidia.com/gpu` in its allocatable resources.

To specifically check for the GPU allocatable key:

```bash
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq '.items[].status.allocatable | select(."nvidia.com/gpu" != null)'
```

## Troubleshooting

### Error: `Unknown runtime handler nvidia`

Check these items:

- `default-runtime: nvidia` is present in `/etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml`.
- The `RuntimeClass` named `nvidia` exists.
- The NVIDIA runtime is present in `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml`.
- `/etc/containerd/conf.d/` is not empty if the K3s template imports configuration from that path.

### GPU Operator does not become ready

If the operator gets stuck on `dcgm-exporter`, disable DCGM components:

```bash
kubectl patch clusterpolicy cluster-policy --type merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"dcgm":{"enabled":false},"dcgmExporter":{"enabled":false}}}'
```

Then re-check the operator pods:

```bash
kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator
```

### Reinstall the operator

If you need a clean reinstall:

```bash
helm uninstall -n gpu-operator $(helm list -n gpu-operator -q)
kubectl delete pods -n gpu-operator --all --grace-period=0 --force
```

Re-run the install command after cleanup.

::: {.callout-note}
Keep API tokens, cloud credentials, and other secrets out of the documentation. Use placeholders such as `<CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN>` in examples.
:::
